name: Sweep Line
description: Process events by sweeping a line from left to right, handling starts and ends of intervals to solve geometric and interval-based problems.
beginnerExplanation: Imagine a vertical line moving from left to right across a number line. At each position, you process 'events' (like the start or end of an interval). This technique eliminates the need to compare every pair and reduces overlap/union/area problems to an O(n log n) solution by sorting events first.
mentalModel: Visualize airport arrivals and departures: sweep time from 00:00 to 24:00. At each event (arrival +1, departure -1), update a running counter. The maximum counter at any point is the peak number of planes at the gate.

At x=2: start event, count=2 (two intervals now overlap)
At x=4: end event, count=1 (first interval ends)
At x=5: start event, count=2 again (new interval begins)

def max_overlap(intervals):
    events = []
    for s, e in intervals:
        events.append((s, 1))
        events.append((e, -1))
    events.sort(key=lambda x: (x[0], x[1]))
    max_count = count = 0
    for _, delta in events:
        count += delta
        max_count = max(max_count, count)
    return max_count

name: Meet in the Middle
description: Split the input into two halves, enumerate all possible states for each half independently, then combine the two half-results to find optimal solutions.
beginnerExplanation: Brute force a problem of size n takes O(2^n). Meet in the Middle splits it into two halves of size n/2, each taking O(2^(n/2)). Then you sort one half and binary-search for complements in it using the other half. This reduces the exponent from n to n/2, which for n=40 is the difference between 1 trillion and 1 million operations.
mentalModel: Two groups of explorers start from opposite sides of a mountain range. Each maps their own half. When they meet in the middle, they compare notes to find the best overall route — far more efficient than one group mapping everything.
learningObjectives: Recognize problems where brute force is O(2^n) but n/2 < 25 (making 2^(n/2) feasible)
Enumerate all subsets for each half and store them
Sort one half and binary-search for complements from the other half
Apply to subset sum, 4-SUM, and closest pair problems

code.python:
def subset_sum_exists(arr, T):
    n = len(arr)
    mid = n // 2
    left_sums = get_all_sums(arr[:mid])
    right_sums = sorted(get_all_sums(arr[mid:]))
    import bisect
    for s in left_sums:
        need = T - s
        idx = bisect.bisect_left(right_sums, need)
        if idx < len(right_sums) and right_sums[idx] == need:
            return True
    return False

def get_all_sums(arr):
    sums = [0]
    for x in arr:
        sums += [s + x for s in sums]
    return sums

name: Lazy Propagation

complexity.time: O(log n) range update, O(log n) query

description: Extend Segment Trees to support O(log n) range updates by deferring (lazily) the propagation of updates to child nodes until they are actually needed.
beginnerExplanation: A standard Segment Tree handles point updates in O(log n). But if you need to add 5 to all elements in a range [l, r], updating every leaf is O(n). Lazy Propagation fixes this: when you update a range, you mark the node as 'dirty' with a pending update. When you later query a child of that node, you push the pending update down just-in-time. This defers work and keeps both updates and queries at O(log n).
mentalModel: Imagine a manager who assigns tasks to teams lazily — they don't tell each team member individually right away. They write a note on the team's board. When an individual needs to check in, the manager first passes on the team note to that person. This deferred distribution is Lazy Propagation.
learningObjectives: Understand why Segment Trees need lazy propagation for range updates
Implement a lazy[] array alongside the segment tree
Know when and how to 'push down' lazy values to children
Handle composition of multiple lazy updates (e.g., add then multiply)

visualWalkthrough: Build segment tree: [10, 3, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4] (node, left-subtree, right-subtree)
Range update [0,1] += 5: Node covers [0,1], mark lazy[node]=5, node value += 5*2=10
Tree root now reflects the update (10+10=20)
Next query [0,1]: visit node, pushDown — send lazy=5 to both leaf children
Leaf 0 becomes 1+5=6, Leaf 1 becomes 2+5=7

complexityReasoning.body: Each range update visits O(log n) nodes (full coverage), marking them lazy instead of propagating deeper. Each query visits O(log n) nodes, pushing down lazily along the way. Both operations are O(log n).

edgeCases: Multiple accumulated lazy values: ensure proper composition (e.g., add before multiply)
Initializing lazy array to 0 (identity element for addition)
Ensure pushDown is called before any query that recurses into children

code.python:
class LazySegTree:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        self.tree = [0] * (4 * n)
        self.lazy = [0] * (4 * n)
    def push_down(self, node, s, e):
        if self.lazy[node]:
            mid = (s + e) // 2
            self.tree[2*node] += self.lazy[node] * (mid - s + 1)
            self.tree[2*node+1] += self.lazy[node] * (e - mid)
            self.lazy[2*node] += self.lazy[node]
            self.lazy[2*node+1] += self.lazy[node]
            self.lazy[node] = 0
    def update(self, node, s, e, l, r, val):
        if r < s or e < l: return
        if l <= s <= e <= r:
            self.tree[node] += val * (e - s + 1)
            self.lazy[node] += val
            return
        self.push_down(node, s, e)
        mid = (s + e) // 2
        self.update(2*node, s, mid, l, r, val)
        self.update(2*node+1, mid+1, e, l, r, val)
        self.tree[node] = self.tree[2*node] + self.tree[2*node+1]
    def query(self, node, s, e, l, r):
        if r < s or e < l: return 0
        if l <= s <= e <= r: return self.tree[node]
        self.push_down(node, s, e)
        mid = (s + e) // 2
        return self.query(2*node, s, mid, l, r) + self.query(2*node+1, mid+1, e, l, r)

name: Z-Algorithm
description: Computes the Z-array where Z[i] is the length of the longest substring starting from index i that matches a prefix of the string. Enables powerful O(n) pattern matching.

This lets you find a pattern P in text T in O(n+m) by creating string P+'$'+T and checking where Z[i] equals len(P).

name: Manacher's Algorithm
description: Finds all palindromic substrings in O(n) using a center-expansion approach with a 'mirror trick' to reuse previously computed palindrome radii.
beginnerExplanation: Checking all palindromes naively is O(n²). Manacher's inserts '#' separators between characters to unify odd/even palindromes, then sweeps left to right. For each center, it uses the rightmost palindrome discovered so far as a 'mirror' to get a free head start on the radius — avoiding redundant comparisons. The result is an array p[] where p[i] is the radius of the longest palindrome centered at i.
mentalModel: Like Z-algorithm, but for palindromes. You maintain a rightmost palindrome [C, R]. For new centers inside R, you get a free mirror-start from p[2C-i]. This 'umbrella' effect makes each character part of at most two radius expansions total, giving O(n).
learningObjectives: Transform string with '#' separators to handle even-length palindromes uniformly
Understand the center C and right boundary R of the rightmost palindrome
Apply the mirror trick: p[i] = min(R-i, p[2C-i]) as a starting radius
Extract original palindrome info from the transformed string's p-array

No: actual center i=3 in transformed → original center 3//2=1, length=3 → 'abba' (length 2*3+1-1... use (p[i]-1)/2... length=p[i]=3 means 3 original chars on each side → 'abba' all 4).

complexityReasoning.body: Each character in the transformed string (length 2n+1) participates in at most one 'new comparison' as the right boundary R expands. Once R moves past a character, it's never re-examined. Total comparisons = O(n), space O(n) for p-array.

code.python:
def manacher(s):
    t = '#' + '#'.join(s) + '#'
    n = len(t)
    p = [0] * n
    c = r = 0
    for i in range(n):
        mirror = 2 * c - i
        if i < r:
            p[i] = min(r - i, p[mirror])
        while i + p[i] + 1 < n and i - p[i] - 1 >= 0 and t[i+p[i]+1] == t[i-p[i]-1]:
            p[i] += 1
        if i + p[i] > r:
            c, r = i, i + p[i]
    max_r = max(p)
    center = p.index(max_r)
    start = (center - max_r) // 2
    return s[start:start + max_r]

name: Interval Tree

name: Order Statistic Tree
description: An augmented BST (typically a Red-Black Tree) where each node also stores the size of its subtree, enabling O(log n) rank and select queries alongside standard BST operations.
beginnerExplanation: A normal BST lets you find if a value exists in O(log n). But asking 'what is the rank (position) of value x?' or 'what is the k-th smallest element?' would be O(n). An Order Statistic Tree adds a size field to each node. size[node] = size[left] + size[right] + 1. With this, rank and select become O(log n) by counting left subtree sizes as you traverse.
mentalModel: A leaderboard where each entry knows exactly how many people are ranked below them. With this count, you can instantly answer 'what position is Alice?' (rank query) or 'who is ranked 5th?' (select query) without scanning all entries.

name: Bloom Filter
description: A space-efficient probabilistic data structure that tests whether an element is a member of a set. False positives are possible, false negatives are not.
beginnerExplanation: A Bloom Filter is a large bit array of m bits and k hash functions. To insert 'apple': hash it k times to get k bit positions, set all those bits to 1. To check if 'mango' exists: hash it k times — if ALL k bits are 1, 'mango' MIGHT be in the set (could be a false positive). If ANY bit is 0, 'mango' is DEFINITELY NOT in the set. Used in databases, CDNs, and spell checkers where memory is critical.
mentalModel: A Bloom Filter is like a nightclub stamp. When you enter, you get k stamps on k different spots on your arm. To check if you've been before, staff checks if all k spots are stamped. Someone else might have the same k spots stamped by coincidence (false positive), but if any spot is missing, you've never been there.
learningObjectives: Understand the trade-off: no false negatives, but possible false positives
Know how to calculate optimal m (bit array size) and k (hash functions) for a target false positive rate p
Formula: m = -n*ln(p) / (ln2)², k = (m/n)*ln2
Know that Bloom Filters do not support deletion (unless using Counting Bloom Filter)

name: Skip List
description: A probabilistic layered linked list that achieves O(log n) average search, insertion, and deletion by maintaining multiple levels of linked lists, each a subset of the level below.
beginnerExplanation: A Skip List is like an express train system. Level 0 is the local train (all stops). Level 1 skips some stops. Level 2 skips more. Level 3 is the express (very few stops). To find element 70: take the express train as far as possible, drop down to the next level, continue. This achieves O(log n) average case without the rotations needed by balanced BSTs.
mentalModel: Imagine a phone book but with multiple layers of indexes: an express index (every 100th entry), a regional index (every 10th entry), and the full list. To find a name, start with the express index, narrow down, then use the detailed list. This multi-level structure is a Skip List.

Know that each element is promoted to level k with probability p^k (usually p=0.5)

name: LSM Tree

complexity.time: O(1) amortized write, O(log n) read

description: Log-Structured Merge-Tree: optimizes write throughput by buffering writes in memory, flushing sorted runs to disk, and periodically merging them. Used in LevelDB, RocksDB, Cassandra, and HBase.
beginnerExplanation: Traditional B-Trees update data in-place on disk, which causes many random I/Os (slow). LSM Trees instead buffer all writes in memory (MemTable), and periodically flush sorted blocks (SSTables) to disk in sequential order (fast!). Reads must check MemTable + multiple SSTables, so reads are slower but writes are dramatically faster. This is a write-optimized structure.
mentalModel: Imagine a whiteboard (MemTable) where you quickly jot new notes. When it's full, you copy everything to a sorted filing cabinet drawer (SSTable). When too many drawers pile up, you merge them into one larger drawer. Reading means checking the whiteboard first, then the drawers.
learningObjectives: Understand the MemTable (in-memory sorted structure, usually a Red-Black Tree or Skip List)
Know that flushes create immutable SSTables (sorted files on disk)
Understand Compaction: merging multiple SSTables to reduce read amplification
Know the read/write/space amplification trade-offs for LSM Trees

name: K-D Tree

complexity.time: O(log n) avg nearest-neighbor, O(n^(1-1/k)) worst

description: A binary tree for organizing k-dimensional points, enabling efficient nearest-neighbor searches and range queries in multiple dimensions.
beginnerExplanation: A K-D Tree (k-dimensional tree) is like a multidimensional binary search tree. At each level, you split points by alternating dimensions: level 0 splits by X, level 1 by Y, level 2 by Z (for 3D), etc. To find the nearest neighbor to a query point, you traverse the tree using the current dimension's split, pruning branches that are farther than the current best distance.
mentalModel: Imagine dividing a 2D map first with a vertical line (by X), then each half with horizontal lines (by Y), then each quarter with vertical lines again. To find the nearest store to your location, you start in your quadrant and prune any areas that can't possibly be closer than the best store you've found so far.

Build a K-D Tree by median splitting along alternating dimensions

code.python:
class KDNode:
    def __init__(self, point):
        self.point = point
        self.left = self.right = None

def build_kd_tree(points, depth=0):
    if not points: return None
    k = len(points[0])
    axis = depth % k
    points.sort(key=lambda p: p[axis])
    mid = len(points) // 2
    node = KDNode(points[mid])
    node.left = build_kd_tree(points[:mid], depth+1)
    node.right = build_kd_tree(points[mid+1:], depth+1)
    return node

def dist(a, b):
    return sum((x-y)**2 for x,y in zip(a,b)) ** 0.5

def nearest_neighbor(root, target, depth=0, best=None):
    if not root: return best
    d = dist(root.point, target)
    if best is None or d < best[1]:
        best = (root.point, d)
    axis = depth % len(target)
    diff = target[axis] - root.point[axis]
    near = root.left if diff < 0 else root.right
    far = root.right if diff < 0 else root.left
    best = nearest_neighbor(near, target, depth+1, best)
    if abs(diff) < best[1]:
        best = nearest_neighbor(far, target, depth+1, best)
    return best

name: Fast & Slow Pointer Pattern
description: Use two pointers at different speeds (tortoise and hare) to detect cycles, find midpoints, and solve various linked list problems without extra space.
beginnerExplanation: Move two pointers through a data structure: slow moves 1 step at a time, fast moves 2 steps. If there's a cycle, fast will eventually lap slow and they'll meet. If not, fast reaches the end. When fast reaches the end, slow is exactly at the middle. This single mechanism solves cycle detection, finding the middle node, and more.
mentalModel: Two runners on a circular track: one twice as fast. If there's a loop, the fast runner will eventually catch up from behind. On a straight track, when the fast runner hits the end, the slow runner is at the halfway point.
learningObjectives: Recognize when fast-slow pointers solve cycle detection (Floyd's algorithm)
Use fast-slow to find the middle of a linked list
Identify the start of a cycle after detection
Apply to 'happy number' and similar problems involving value cycles

Step 1: slow→2, fast→3 (fast jumps 2)
Step 2: slow→3, fast→5
Step 3: slow→4, fast→4 (met!). Cycle confirmed.
Find cycle start: reset slow to head, advance both 1 step → meet at node 3

complexityReasoning.body: Each pointer traverses at most O(n) nodes before meeting (or fast reaching null). Detection + finding start = O(n). Space O(1) — only two pointers needed.

edgeCases: Empty list: return false/null
Single node with self-loop: fast.next = fast → detect on first step
No cycle: fast reaches null, return false

name: Merge Interval Pattern
description: Sort intervals by start time, then merge overlapping intervals in a single linear sweep. Recognizes when intervals can be collapsed or extended.
beginnerExplanation: Sort intervals by start. Keep a running 'current' interval. For each next interval: if it overlaps current (next.start ≤ current.end), merge them by taking max(current.end, next.end). If it doesn't overlap, push current to result and start fresh. The sort makes this a linear scan after O(n log n) sorting.
mentalModel: Imagine scheduling meetings and combining any that overlap into a single longer block. Sort all meetings by start time. Walk through and extend the last meeting's end time whenever the next meeting overlaps. When there's a gap, the block is finalized.
learningObjectives: Sort by start time to make overlaps detectable in order
Recognize overlap condition: next.start <= current.end
Merge by extending end: max(current.end, next.end)

End of list → finalize [15,18]. Result: [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]

Single interval: return as-is

name: Cyclic Sort Pattern
description: Place each number at its correct index position in O(n) time by cycling through misplaced elements. Ideal for problems with numbers in range [1,n].
beginnerExplanation: If you have an array with numbers 1 to n, each number belongs at index (number-1). Cyclic Sort: iterate through the array. If arr[i] is not at its correct index, swap arr[i] with arr[arr[i]-1]. Keep swapping until arr[i] is in its right place, then move to the next index. After this O(n) pass, any numbers at wrong indices are duplicates or missing.
mentalModel: Think of numbered parking spots 1 to n. If car #5 is in spot 3, move it to spot 5. The car that was in spot 5 goes somewhere else. Repeat until every car is in the correct spot. Then check for empties (missing numbers) or double-parked spots (duplicates).
learningObjectives: Recognize problems involving numbers in range [1,n] as Cyclic Sort candidates
Implement the swap: while arr[i] != i+1, swap arr[i] with arr[arr[i]-1]

No: use arr[i]<n swap. i=0: arr[0]=3≥n=3 → skip. i=1: arr[1]=0, at idx 0≠1 → swap → [0,3,1]. i=1 again: arr[1]=3≥n → skip. i=2: arr[2]=1, at idx 1≠2 → swap → [0,1,3]. i=2: arr[2]=3≥n → skip. name: Heap Pattern (Top K)
description: Use a min-heap or max-heap of size k to efficiently track the top-K largest/smallest elements in a stream or array without sorting the entire collection.
beginnerExplanation: To find the k largest elements: maintain a min-heap of size k. For each new element, add it to the heap. If the heap exceeds size k, remove the minimum (the heap's root). After processing all elements, the heap contains the k largest. The heap keeps the 'current k best' — whenever a better candidate arrives, it evicts the worst of the current k.
mentalModel: Imagine picking the top-3 players from 100 auditions. You keep a 'roster' of the current 3 best. For each new audition, if they're better than the worst current player, they take that spot. At the end, your roster has the top-3. The heap is that roster.

name: Monotonic Queue Pattern
description: A double-ended queue (deque) that maintains elements in monotonically increasing or decreasing order, enabling O(n) sliding window minimum/maximum queries.
beginnerExplanation: For sliding window maximum: maintain a deque that stores indices in decreasing order of their values. For each new element: remove from the back any elements smaller than it (they can never be a future max). Remove from the front any elements that are outside the window. The front always has the current window maximum. Each element is added and removed from the deque at most once: total O(n).
mentalModel: Think of a sliding window with a 'contestant board' that tracks the best candidates. When a stronger contestant arrives, all weaker ones behind them are permanently eliminated (they'll never be needed — the strong one is both newer and better). The champion (front of deque) changes only when they exit the window.
learningObjectives: Understand the monotonic deque invariant: elements in the deque are always in one order
Remove from the back when adding a new element (to maintain order)
Remove from the front when the front falls outside the current window

name: DP Pattern Recognition
description: A systematic framework for identifying dynamic programming problems by recognizing overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure, then choosing between memoization (top-down) and tabulation (bottom-up).
beginnerExplanation: DP applies when: (1) the problem asks for an optimal value (min, max, count) or asks 'is it possible?', (2) decisions at each step affect future choices, and (3) smaller subproblems repeat. Recognition signals: 'minimum number of...', 'number of ways to...', 'maximum profit...'. Once recognized, define state (what uniquely describes a subproblem), write recurrence, and choose memoization or tabulation.
mentalModel: DP is about recognizing that you're solving the same sub-question multiple times. If you could write it as recursion, but the recursion tree has repeated nodes — that's DP. Cache the answers to avoid recomputation.
learningObjectives: Identify DP: overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure
Define the DP state: what parameters uniquely represent a subproblem
Write the recurrence relation (transition function)
Choose memoization (top-down) vs tabulation (bottom-up) and space optimization

workedExample.title: Recognize DP in Climbing Stairs
workedExample.body: Problem: n stairs, 1 or 2 steps each time. How many ways? Signal: 'how many ways' → DP. State: f(n) = ways to reach step n. Recurrence: f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2) (last step was 1 or 2). Base: f(1)=1, f(2)=2. Optimal substructure: ways to n depends only on n-1 and n-2. Overlapping: f(5) needs f(4) and f(3), f(4) also needs f(3)→reuse!

visualWalkthrough: Step 1: Spot the DP signal — 'number of ways', 'minimum cost', 'maximum value'
Step 2: Define state — what variables uniquely identify a subproblem
Step 3: Write recurrence — how does f(n) relate to smaller subproblems?
Step 4: Identify base cases — simplest inputs with known answers
Step 5: Implement — memoization (top-down) or tabulation (bottom-up)

complexityReasoning.body: State space × time per state. For 1D DP with n states and O(1) per state: O(n). For 2D with n×m states: O(n×m). Space: O(n) or O(n×m), often reducible with rolling array.

edgeCases: Empty input or n=0: define carefully (often 1 for counting, 0 for optimization)
All elements same: avoid n×n state space when possible
Large n: check if O(n) state space is feasible before coding O(n²)

name: Backtracking Pattern
description: Systematically explore all possible solutions by building candidates incrementally and abandoning (backtracking) as soon as a candidate cannot lead to a valid solution.
beginnerExplanation: Backtracking is recursion with pruning. At each step, you try all available choices. After making a choice, recurse. If the recursion fails (constraint violated), undo the choice and try the next option. The key insight: backtrack as early as possible to avoid exploring dead-end paths. Template: choose → explore → unchoose.
mentalModel: Solving a maze: at each junction, try left. If you hit a dead end, come back and try right. If all options from this junction are dead ends, backtrack to the previous junction. You systematically eliminate all dead ends until you find the exit (or exhaust all paths).
learningObjectives: Understand the choose-explore-unchoose template
Recognize backtracking problems: permutations, combinations, subsets, N-queens, Sudoku
Identify pruning conditions to early-terminate dead branches
Distinguish backtracking from exhaustive brute force (backtracking prunes)

name: Brute Force First

name: Optimization Strategies
description: A systematic toolkit of techniques for improving time and space complexity: precomputation, sorting, hashing, two pointers, divide and conquer, and more.
beginnerExplanation: After stating brute force, interviewers expect you to optimize. Common strategies: (1) Precompute repeated work (prefix sums, hash maps). (2) Sort to enable binary search or two pointers. (3) Shrink state space with DP. (4) Use monotonic structures (stack/queue) for O(n) window queries. (5) Avoid inner loops by finding the mathematical relationship. Each strategy targets a specific type of redundancy.
mentalModel: Optimization is about identifying what the brute force computes repeatedly and finding a way to compute it once. Ask: 'What does the inner loop do that I could pre-calculate?' or 'Is there an order to process elements that makes later checks trivial?'
learningObjectives: Recognize precomputation opportunities (prefix sums, frequency maps, sorted order)
Understand how sorting changes the search problem
Apply two pointers after sorting to avoid O(n²) pair enumeration
Use monotonic stack/queue for O(n) 'next greater/smaller' problems

workedExample.title: Optimize Subarray Sum = K
workedExample.body: Brute O(n²): try every subarray. Optimization: prefix sum + hash map. Store prefix sum frequencies. For each index r, we want prefix[r]-prefix[l]=K → prefix[l]=prefix[r]-K. Look up prefix[r]-K in hash map: O(1)! Total: O(n). The inner loop (finding prefix[l]) is replaced by a hash map lookup.

visualWalkthrough: Brute force: two nested loops checking all subarrays → O(n²)
Insight: subarray sum = prefix[r] - prefix[l]. We want this = K
So: we need prefix[l] = prefix[r] - K
Precompute: maintain HashMap of prefix sum frequencies
Result: single pass, O(n) time, O(n) space

complexityReasoning.body: Optimization strategies typically improve O(n²) → O(n log n) (via sorting) or O(n²) → O(n) (via hashing/precomputation). Space often trades from O(1) to O(n).

edgeCases: Negative numbers: prefix sum approach still works for sum=K
Sorting destroys index info: save indices before sorting
Hash collisions: use size-aware moduli or known good hash functions

code.python:
# Strategy 1: Precompute (prefix sums + hash map)
from collections import defaultdict
def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    prefix_freq = defaultdict(int)
    prefix_freq[0] = 1
    prefix = count = 0
    for n in nums:
        prefix += n
        count += prefix_freq[prefix - k]
        prefix_freq[prefix] += 1
    return count

# Strategy 2: Sort + two pointers
def two_sum_sorted(nums, target):
    nums.sort()
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums)-1
    while lo < hi:
        s = nums[lo] + nums[hi]
        if s == target: return [lo, hi]
        elif s < target: lo += 1
        else: hi -= 1
    return []

name: Dry Run Technique

Choose a test case small enough to trace but non-trivial (n=3 or 4, not n=0 or n=1).
mentalModel: You are the CPU. Go through your code instruction by instruction, computing exact values. Don't assume — verify. If you think 'the loop should stop at i=5', trace it: what is i after each iteration? Does it actually stop at 5 or 6?

def robust_search(arr, target):
    # Edge case: empty

    # Edge case: single element

    # Main logic

        elif arr[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1

description: Accurately analyze and clearly communicate time and space complexity during interviews, including deriving it live from your solution and explaining the reasoning.

# Template for complexity analysis
# Time: count iterations × work per iteration
# Space: count max memory live at any point

def merge_sort(arr):
    # Time: O(n log n) — log n levels, O(n) per level
    # Space: O(n) auxiliary + O(log n) call stack = O(n)
    if len(arr) <= 1: return arr
    mid = len(arr) // 2
    left = merge_sort(arr[:mid])
    right = merge_sort(arr[mid:])
    return merge(left, right)

def bfs(graph, start):
    # Time: O(V + E) — visit each node + edge once
    # Space: O(V) — visited set + queue
    visited = set([start])
    queue = [start]
    while queue:
        node = queue.pop(0)
        for neighbor in graph[node]:
            if neighbor not in visited:
                visited.add(neighbor)
                queue.append(neighbor)

name: Communication Skills
description: Structure your verbal communication during coding interviews: clarifying the problem, thinking aloud, explaining your approach, and discussing trade-offs.
beginnerExplanation: Top tech companies evaluate not just your code but how you think. 'Silent coders' often fail even with correct solutions. Say what you're thinking: 'I'm considering using a hash map to reduce lookup time from O(n) to O(1).' Ask clarifying questions: 'Can elements be negative? Is the array sorted? What should I return if no answer exists?' This shows collaborative problem-solving skills.
mentalModel: Treat the interview like pair programming. Your interviewer is your pair. You wouldn't code silently in pair programming — you'd explain your thinking, ask questions, and discuss alternatives. Do the same in an interview.
learningObjectives: Start by clarifying inputs, outputs, constraints, and edge cases
Verbalize your thinking before coding: state the approach and complexity
Explain what each part of your code does as you write it
After coding, summarize complexity and proactively mention limitations or improvements

workedExample.title: Communication Template for an Interview Problem
workedExample.body: 1. Restate: 'So I need to find the maximum sum subarray — correct?' 2. Clarify: 'Can all elements be negative? What's the expected output in that case?' 3. Approach: 'My brute force would be O(n²). I can optimize using Kadane's algorithm to O(n) because...' 4. Code with narration: 'maxEndingHere tracks the max sum subarray ending at current index...' 5. Verify: 'Let me dry run on [−2,1,−3,4,−1,2,1,−5,4]. Expected output: 6.' 6. Complexity: 'Time O(n), Space O(1).'

visualWalkthrough: Phase 1 (2 min): Clarify problem, constraints, edge cases
Phase 2 (3 min): State brute force, then optimal approach with reasoning
Phase 3 (15 min): Code while narrating each decision
Phase 4 (3 min): Dry run on example, state complexity
Phase 5 (2 min): Discuss edge cases and potential improvements

complexityReasoning.body: Communication skills don't have algorithmic complexity but they heavily influence interview outcomes. Studies show interviewers rate clear communicators ~20-30% higher even with equivalent code quality.

edgeCases: Clarify before coding, not after discovering an issue mid-implementation
If stuck, say so: 'I'm not sure about the optimal approach yet — let me think through brute force first'

# Communication checklist before coding:
# [ ] Restated the problem correctly?
# [ ] Clarified input format and constraints?
# [ ] Handled edge cases (empty, single, negatives, overflow)?
# [ ] Stated brute force and its complexity?
# [ ] Explained optimization and why it works?
# [ ] Coded with narration?
# [ ] Dry run on at least one example?
# [ ] Stated final time and space complexity?
# [ ] Asked if interviewer has questions?

def communicate_while_coding(arr, target):
    # 'I'll initialize two pointers after sorting'
    arr.sort()  # 'Sort costs O(n log n) which will dominate'
    left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1  # 'Both start at extremes'
    while left < right:
        s = arr[left] + arr[right]
        if s == target: return True  # 'Found a pair'
        elif s < target: left += 1  # 'Too small, need larger'
        else: right -= 1            # 'Too large, need smaller'
    return False

name: Mock Interview Strategy
description: How to set up, run, and extract maximum learning from mock interviews to simulate real interview pressure and identify gaps in your preparation.
beginnerExplanation: Mock interviews are the single highest-ROI activity in interview preparation. They simulate real pressure, reveal unknown weaknesses, and train you to code while speaking. One mock interview is worth reading 10 more Leetcode solutions. How to do them effectively: time yourself strictly (20-25 min per problem), explain out loud throughout, have a partner give feedback on communication not just correctness, and debrief immediately after.
mentalModel: Athletes train by simulating the actual game conditions — sprinters time themselves, tennis players practice match play. Coding interviews are the same: solving Leetcode silently is training dribbling alone; mock interviews are practice matches.
learningObjectives: Use timed practice: 20-25 minutes per medium problem, 35-45 for hard
Practice speaking while coding — don't code silently
Use platforms like Pramp, Interviewing.io, or peer mock interviews
Debrief after each mock: what pattern did I miss? What edge case did I forget? Was my communication clear?

workedExample.title: Mock Interview Debrief Template
workedExample.body: Problem: Longest Palindromic Substring. My approach: Expand around center O(n²). Optimal: Manacher O(n). What I missed: didn't ask about input constraints (could n be 0?). Communication gap: silent while expanding, should have narrated. Time: took 28 min (too long). Next action: practice 3 more palindrome problems, work on narrating expand-around-center pattern.

visualWalkthrough: Week 1: Solve 30 easy problems, identify 5 core patterns you know well
Week 2-3: Solve 50 medium problems (2-3 per day), pattern-tag each
Week 4: Start mock interviews (2 per week minimum)
Week 5-6: 4+ mock interviews per week, focus on communication
Final week: Review hard problems, system design if needed, mental prep

complexityReasoning.body: Mock interview prep is O(n) in the number of problems practiced. Effectiveness is O(quality × quantity). Mocks provide the quality multiplier that solo practice cannot.

edgeCases: Too few mocks: not enough pressure simulation
Too many mocks without review: reinforces bad habits
Only easy problems: builds false confidence

name: Rabin-Karp
description: A string search algorithm using rolling hash to find a pattern in text in O(n+m) average time. Computes the hash of the pattern once, then rolls the hash across the text by subtracting the outgoing character and adding the incoming one.
beginnerExplanation: Instead of comparing each character when the window slides, Rabin-Karp computes a number (hash) representing the current window. When hashes match, it verifies character-by-character. The rolling hash update is O(1) — just subtract the old left character and add the new right character — making the amortized cost nearly linear.
mentalModel: Think of a window of glass sliding across a wall of tiles. Instead of reading each tile letter in the window, you have a running score that changes as the window moves. Only when the score matches the target do you actually read the tiles.
learningObjectives: Understand polynomial rolling hash and why it enables O(1) window updates
Compute the initial hash for a pattern in O(m)
Roll the hash across the text in O(1) per step
Handle hash collisions with character-by-character verification

workedExample.title: Find 'abc' in 'xabcyz'
workedExample.body: BASE=31, MOD=1e9+7. Hash('abc')=97+98*31+99*961=... Compute initial window hash for 'xab'. Slide: subtract 'x'*BASE^2, add 'c'. When hash matches, verify character by character. Found at index 1!

visualWalkthrough: Compute hash(pattern) in O(m)
Compute hash of first m characters of text
Compare hashes: if match, verify character by character
Roll hash: subtract contribution of leftmost char, add rightmost char
Repeat until end of text — average O(1) per step

complexityReasoning.body: Average O(n+m): hash computation is O(m), each window slide is O(1), and hash collisions are rare. Worst case O(nm) if every window causes a false hash match (very unlikely with good hash functions). Space O(1) as rolling hash uses only constant variables.

edgeCases: Pattern longer than text: return immediately
Multiple occurrences: keep searching after first match
Hash collision: always verify by character comparison when hashes match
Single character pattern: simplifies to linear scan
